subject: social-studies
title: Neighbourhood Change: One Site, Stage by Stage
objectives: Explain how a neighbourhood changes in stages: low-rise houses and open ground, transport links arriving first, housing blocks rising plot by plot, shops, a market and a school opening as families move in
Name what arrives at each stage and why the population bar climbs at every stage
Explain why a neighbourhood does not change all at once, and why transport arrives before homes

definitions.meaning: The area around a home - its houses, shops, schools and transport - that changes stage by stage as people move in and new buildings and services arrive.
The small first homes on the site: a few low-rise houses standing on open ground, home to only a few families at the start.
The empty land on the site at the start, where the housing blocks later rise plot by plot.
The ways of reaching the site that arrive first: the MRT station and the bus stop, which open before the housing blocks rise.
The tall blocks of flats that rise plot by plot on the open ground after transport arrives, bringing many more families into the neighbourhood.
The bar in the animation that shows how many people live here: it climbs at every stage as more families arrive, and never jumps in one step.

mechanismSteps: Stage 1: the site as found - houses and open ground - a few low-rise houses stand on open ground, only a few families live here, and the population bar is at its lowest (s1).
Stage 2: transport arrives first - MRT station and bus stop - the station and bus stop open so the site is easy to reach, and the population bar climbs one step (s2).

Stage 3: blocks rise, then shops, a market and a school open - housing blocks rise plot by plot, families move into the flats, and the shops, market and school open to serve them as the population bar climbs again (s3).

Stage 4: the wrong turn, corrected - change happens stage by stage - everything flashes in together, then the true sequence is replayed in order and the population bar climbs at every stage to full (s4).
workedExample: Work through the whole change in order. Stage 1 (s1): the site as found - a few low-rise houses on open ground, with only a few families living here. Stage 2 (s2): transport arrives first - an MRT station and a bus stop open, so the site is easy to reach. Transport arrives before homes: that order is what lets the later stages work. Stage 3 (s3): housing blocks rise plot by plot on the open ground, and as families move into the flats, shops, a market and a school open to serve them. Stage 4 (s4): the all-at-once wrong turn is played out and corrected, and the true sequence is replayed with the population bar climbing at every stage. At every stage the order is the same: open ground, transport first, blocks plot by plot, then shops, market and school as families arrive.

trap.misconception: A neighbourhood changes all at once, because the new flats, shops and MRT station all appear in a single step.
trap.explanation: The slip: Before-and-after photographs of a neighbourhood look completely different, so it is easy to imagine the old houses were swept away and the flats, shops and station put in their place overnight. The fix: A neighbourhood changes stage by stage: transport links arrive first as the MRT station and bus stop open, housing blocks then rise plot by plot, and only as families move in do the shops, market and school open - the population grows at every stage, not in one jump. In class, replay scene 2: freeze at the MRT station and bus stop and ask why transport arrives before homes, then run scene 4 and contrast the all-at-once flash with the corrected stage-by-stage replay.
